analysis.one_liner: Bans fees on paid-in-full balances, requires rate-hike notices, and ends double-cycle credit card billing.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned several credit card fee practices, was never brought to a vote: after its March 1999 introduction it went to a House committee and subcommittee and stayed there until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to stop several credit card practices that raise cardholders' costs. It would have banned fees charged to people who pay their balance in full and on time, required 15 days' advance notice before an interest rate increase, and let cardholders who cancel keep the old rate on the balance they already owed. It also would have required clear disclosure of fees on convenience checks, banned fees on transactions the card issuer itself approved, ended double-cycle billing that charges interest on already-paid balances, and required statements to show how long debt takes to pay off at the minimum payment.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary credit cardholders, especially people who carry a balance or get hit with surprise rate increases, penalty fees, or charges for paying in full. Anyone who received convenience checks or teaser-rate offers would get clearer, more prominent disclosures of what those actually cost.

how_it_helps.text: Bars creditors from charging a minimum finance charge or fee solely because a cardholder repaid credit in full before the grace period [S3].
Requires at least 15 days' advance notice of any interest rate increase and lets the cardholder cancel before it takes effect, keeping the old rate on the outstanding balance after cancellation [S3].
Prohibits raising the rate or fees on a canceled card's outstanding balance after cancellation [S2].
Requires prominent disclosure of transaction fees and interest rates on convenience checks used to move credit to a third party [S3].
Bars over-the-limit fees on transactions the creditor approved in advance or at the time of the transaction [S3].
Prohibits two-cycle billing, which lets issuers charge interest on balances that were already paid during the previous cycle [S2].

Requires disclosures on teaser rates naming the permanent rate and date it takes effect, prominent notice of the payment due date before late fees, and a statement of how many years it takes to pay off a balance if only the minimum is paid [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks, which earn revenue from fees on paid-in-full accounts, two-cycle billing, over-limit fees on approved transactions, and rate increases applied without notice to existing balances. Some of that revenue loss would likely be offset through other fees, rates, or reduced access to credit for higher-risk borrowers.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: banning fee and interest practices unilaterally can push issuers to raise headline interest rates, tighten credit standards, or add annual fees, shifting costs to all borrowers including those who pay on time. The bill itself acknowledges issuers might respond this way by explicitly preserving flat annual fees charged in advance [S3].
The bill adds significant new disclosure paperwork for issuers on convenience checks, teaser rates, and payment due dates, costs that could be passed along to customers [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill only mandates notice, not approval: cardholders facing a rate increase could still keep their account, but they had to act within 15 days and surrender their cards to lock in the old rate on the balance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly targeted practices widely seen as unfair traps—fees for paying on time, retroactive rate increases, interest on already-paid balances, and minimum payments that never reduce debt. The main tradeoff is that issuers would recover some lost revenue elsewhere, potentially through higher rates or annual fees, which would hit all borrowers. On balance, the protections aimed at practices that cost cardholders real money with little offsetting benefit, but the bill never advanced far enough for its actual costs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1999 and sent to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, where it stayed with no hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Roybal-Allard introduced the bill on March 24, 1999, with 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services [S5].
On April 16, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and never received a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].
The bill attracted 25 cosponsors (24 Democrats and 1 Republican) [S4], but committee leadership never advanced it to a markup or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and banks kept practices like fees on paid-in-full accounts, double-cycle billing, and unannounced rate increases for another decade—until a later Congress (the CARD Act of 2009) imposed similar protections. Cardholders continued paying those fees in the meantime.

for.name: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Consumer Protection Act of 1999 and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: 25 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 24 Democrats and 1 Republican.

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on April 16, 1999, and held no markup or hearing that advanced the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsors split 24 Democrats to 1 Republican [S4], but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of any floor decision is unknown.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer banks
industries.note: The bill would have cut off several revenue streams: fees on cardholders who pay in full, two-cycle billing interest, over-limit fees on transactions the issuer approved, and rate increases applied retroactively to balances without notice. Its interest ran directly against cardholders' pocketbooks, which is why the bill was framed as consumer protection.
